'''Arthur Baraway Komar''' (March 26, 1931 – June 3, 2011) known as '''Art Komar''' was an American [[theoretical physicist]], specializing in [[general relativity]] and helping to develop the [[Canonical quantum gravity|canonical approach]] to [[quantum gravity]]. Arthur Komar made a significant contribution to physics as an educator, research scientist, and administrator. He had wide interests in numerous other subjects, and his friends knew him as a [[Renaissance man]].<ref name=":0">{{Cite web |title=Newsletter (Archives – This Week in Physics) – Physics – Answers |url=https://answers.syr.edu/pages/viewpage.action?pageId=118785607&preview=/118785607/118785616/6+Volume.pdf |access-date=2023-09-15 |website=answers.syr.edu}}</ref> The terms [[Komar mass]] and [[Komar superpotential]] are named after him.

==Life and education==
Arthur "Artie" Komar attended [[Midwood High School]] in [[Brooklyn]], where he was a capable student and chose to specialize in physics before going on to study physics at [[Princeton University|Princeton]] on a Hibben scholarship in 1948.<ref name=":1">{{Cite web |date=2016-01-21 |title=Arthur B. Komar '52 *56 |url=https://paw.princeton.edu/memorial/arthur-b-komar-%E2%80%9952-56 |access-date=2023-09-15 |website=Princeton Alumni Weekly |language=en}}</ref> While there, he wrote for Nassau literary magazine, was a four-year member of the [[American Whig–Cliosophic Society|Whig-Clio senate]], and was elected to the [[Phi Beta Kappa]] Society at the end of his junior year, graduating in 1952 and with an undergraduate thesis reviewing the classical electron.<ref name=":1" /><ref name=":0" /> That year he married Dolly Rothziege, a German-born artist who was 18 years old at the time, and with whom he later had two children.<ref name=":2">{{Cite web |last=Komar Honig |first=The Estate of Dolly Komar Honig |date=2021 |title=About Dolly Komar Honig |url=https://www.dollykomarhonig.com/about |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230915143727/https://www.dollykomarhonig.com/about |archive-date=15 September 2023 |access-date=15 September 2023 |website=About Dolly Komar Honig}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=Home – Sisskind Funeral Service, LLC. |url=https://sisskindfuneralservice.com/home/display.php?id=2929 |access-date=2023-09-15 |website=sisskindfuneralservice.com}}</ref> Komar went on to do his PhD at Princeton under the direction of [[John Archibald Wheeler]], which he received in 1956 for a thesis entitled, ''Some Consequences of [[Mach's principle|Mach's Principle]] for General Relativity''.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Komar |first1=Arthur Baraway |year=1956 |title=Some Consequences of Mach's Principle for the General Theory of Relativity, Thesis (Ph.D.) |location=Princeton University |publisher=[[Dissertations Abstracts International]] |volume=17-06 |page=1360 |bibcode=1956PhDT........28K}}</ref>

After graduating, Komar and his wife moved for one year to the [[Niels Bohr Institute]] at [[University of Copenhagen]], where he was a Fellow of the [[American-Scandinavian Foundation]]. The family's first child was born in 1957, a son, and soon after they moved so Komar could join [[Syracuse University]].<ref name=":2" /> He began as a postdoc, soon rising to the ranks of assistant professor and then associate professor.<ref name=":1" /> The Komars had their second child in 1962, and shortly left to return to New York City so that Komar could join the physics faculty of [[Yeshiva University]] as an associate professor in 1963, later becoming full professor.<ref>{{Cite book |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=HxlbAAAAYAAJ&dq=%22artie+komar%22+physics&pg=RA2-PA32 |title=Princeton Alumni Weekly |date=1969 |publisher=Princeton University Press |language=en}}</ref><ref name=":2" /> From 1969 until 1978 Komar was the dean of Yeshiva's [[Belfer Graduate School of Science of Yeshiva University|Belfer Graduate School of Science]].<ref>{{Cite book |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=HxlbAAAAYAAJ&dq=%22artie+komar%22&pg=RA2-PA32 |title=Princeton Alumni Weekly |date=1969 |publisher=Princeton University Press |language=en}}</ref> Komar became chair of the physics department in Yeshiva from 1978 to 1982 and chairman of the Division of Natural Science from 1983 to 1986. He also served as a physics program director at the [[National Science Foundation]],<ref name=":1" /> during which time Komar awarded a quantum gravity grant to physicist and author [[Carlo Rovelli]] while the latter was at the [[University of Pittsburgh]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=NSF Award Search: Award # 9012099 – Non-Perturbative Quantum Gravity (Physics) |url=https://www.nsf.gov/awardsearch/showAward?AWD_ID=9012099&HistoricalAwards=false |access-date=2023-09-15 |website=www.nsf.gov}}</ref> Komar was a consultant for the [[LIGO]] project from 1991 to 1992.<ref name=":0" />

In 1974 Arthur and Dolly were divorced. Dolly moved back to [[Syracuse, New York|Syracuse]], where she married an old family friend and Syracuse University physicist, [[Arnold Honig]].<ref name=":2" /> Meanwhile, developmental psychologist at Syracuse University [[Alice Sterling Honig]], who was Arnold Honig's ex-wife, became the long-term partner of Arthur Komar until he died.<ref name=":2" /> Komar retired in 1997 and moved back to Syracuse,<ref name=":0" /> where he died on 3 June 2011 at the age of 80.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Arthur Komar Obituary (2011) – Syracuse, NY – Syracuse Post Standard |url=https://obits.syracuse.com/us/obituaries/syracuse/name/arthur-komar-obituary?id=26642684 |access-date=2023-09-15 |website=Legacy.com}}</ref>

==Research==
[[File:Ray-Sachs-Ivor-Robinson-Art-Komar-and-John-Lighton-Synge-Jablonna-1962-Photo.png|thumb|''From left:'' [[Rainer Sachs]], [[Ivor Robinson (physicist)|Ivor Robinson]], Komar,  [[John Lighton Synge]], in 1962]]
Komar's interests in physics ranged over numerous fundamental and applied concepts, including [[Conserved quantity|conserved quantities]], [[space and time]], and [[thermodynamics]]. Notably he pursued the problem of [[observable]]s in general relativity and in quantum theory.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Komar |first=Arthur |date=1958-08-15 |title=Construction of a Complete Set of Independent Observables in the General Theory of Relativity |url=https://link.aps.org/doi/10.1103/PhysRev.111.1182 |journal=Physical Review |volume=111 |issue=4 |pages=1182–1187 |doi=10.1103/PhysRev.111.1182|bibcode=1958PhRv..111.1182K |url-access=subscription }}</ref>

It is said that John Wheeler arranged a tea-time visit for his class, which to Arthur's pleasure had the company of [[Albert Einstein]].<ref name=":1" /> Throughout his scientific career, Arthur remained fond of Princeton.<ref name=":1" />

Beginning in the late 1950s Komar developed a fruitful collaboration with [[Peter Bergmann]], working together to help develop the foundations of [[canonical quantum gravity]], and in particular the use of [[Hamilton-Jacobi theory]] to define a reduced [[phase space]] for general relativity with the [[diffeomorphism group]] as its [[Gauge group (mathematics)|gauge group]] in the 1960s and 1970s.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Thiemann |first=Thomas |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=p-sXBRd1i0IC&dq=%22komar%22+canonical+quantum+gravity&pg=PA39 |title=Modern Canonical Quantum General Relativity |date=2008-11-13 |publisher=Cambridge University Press |isbn=978-1-139-46759-9 |language=en}}</ref> This approach is notable for its use of [[Weyl curvature]] scalars to determine a time-dependent gauge fixing.<ref name=":3">{{Cite journal |last1=Pons |first1=J. M. |last2=Salisbury |first2=D. C. |date=2005-06-06 |title=Issue of time in generally covariant theories and the Komar-Bergmann approach to observables in general relativity |url=https://link.aps.org/doi/10.1103/PhysRevD.71.124012 |journal=Physical Review D |volume=71 |issue=12 |article-number=124012 |doi=10.1103/PhysRevD.71.124012|arxiv=gr-qc/0503013 |bibcode=2005PhRvD..71l4012P |hdl=2445/12486 |hdl-access=free }}</ref>

Komar also worked on the problem of [[Invariant (physics)|invariant]]s in general relativistic spacetimes, now known as Komar-invariants or Bergmann-Komar invariants.<ref name=":3" />

Komar is also known for formulating the concept of [[Komar mass]] and [[Komar superpotential]].
